question: I feel really lonely since I became Muslim. Is that normal?
answer: Yes. Many new Muslims feel lonely, especially in the first months. Old friendships can change, and a new community can take time to feel like home. A Yaqeen Institute survey of American converts found that masjids, imams and Muslim friendships matter a lot, and that converts need support long after the day they say the Shahada. Start small: one class, one friendly face, one regular visit. If the loneliness turns into hopelessness, please talk to someone now (call or text 9-8-8 in Canada).

question: How do I know who I can trust for help?
answer: Start with organisations, not individuals you just met. A good sign is an organisation that has a public program page, an office phone or email, and is happy for you to ask other teachers too. Be careful with anyone who asks for money, wants to rush you into marriage, tells you to keep things secret, or tries to cut you off from family or other Muslims. For non-religious needs such as housing, food or counselling in Ontario, 211 is confidential and answered 24/7 (call or text 2-1-1). For religious rulings about your own situation, ask a qualified local imam.

question: Is there a program for new Muslims in Ottawa?
answer: Yes. Islam Care Centre in downtown Ottawa (currently at 375 Somerset St. W) runs a free weekly program called Convert Care, which it describes as covering the basics new Muslims need to know. Its page says it meets every Wednesday at 6:00 pm. Schedules change, so call the centre at (613) 232-0210 before your first visit. You are welcome to go just to listen.

question: I went to the masjid and nobody talked to me. Did I do something wrong?
answer: Almost certainly not. Communities are made of ordinary people, and sometimes they are busy, shy, or do not realise you are new. New Muslim Academy puts it simply: communities are imperfect, and your faith does not depend on how one group received you. Try again at a quieter time, introduce yourself to the office or the imam, or ask whether the masjid has a new Muslim program. If one place does not feel right, it is fine to try another.

question: Can I talk to a Muslim counsellor?
answer: Yes. Several Canadian organisations offer faith-aware support. Naseeha runs a Muslim youth helpline at 1 (866) 627-3342. Nisa Helpline offers free peer support for women and girls 14 and up at +1 888 711 6472, 8 am to midnight Eastern. For ongoing therapy, Khalil Center (online, 416-901-2244) and Muslim Family Services of Ottawa (613-562-2273) have professional counsellors; ask about fees and insurance. None of these replace 911 or 9-8-8 in an emergency.

question: How can I tell if food in a Canadian store is really halal?
answer: In Canada, a label that says or suggests 'halal' must also name the person or organisation that certified it. That is a federal labelling rule enforced by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency. The government does not decide what counts as halal, so the next step is yours: look for the certifier's name, then check whether your local masjid trusts that certifier. Common names you will see in Ontario include the Halal Monitoring Authority (HMA) and ISNA Canada Halal, and their standards are not identical. If a shop or restaurant says 'halal' with no certifier, you can politely ask to see the certificate.
differences: Certifiers differ on machine slaughter and stunning.

question: What food is actually forbidden for Muslims?
answer: The Quran names a short list: animals that died on their own, blood, pork, and meat dedicated to anything other than Allah. Alcohol and other intoxicants are also forbidden. Vegetables, fruit, grains, eggs and fish are generally fine. Some cheeses and other dairy products use animal enzymes, so check those. Many new Muslims start with simple foods like these while they learn the rest. The Quran also says that if you are truly forced by need, you are not sinful, so there is no need to panic.
differences: Details about seafood and some animals differ between the schools.

question: Is vanilla extract or food with a little alcohol in the ingredients okay?
answer: Drinking alcohol is clearly forbidden. Tiny amounts of alcohol used as a solvent in flavourings such as vanilla extract are a real difference of opinion among scholars. In the Hanafi school, as explained by SeekersGuidance, non-wine alcohol in something like vanilla is allowed if it is not used to get intoxicated and the amount cannot intoxicate, though choosing alcohol-free vanilla is the more careful option. Other scholars are stricter and avoid any added alcohol, and certifiers set their own rules. While you are new, it is fine to pick alcohol-free versions where they are easy to find, and to ask your local imam which view your community follows.
differences: The Hanafi school allows small amounts of non-wine alcohol used this way. Many other scholars do not.

question: Do I need to avoid gelatin?
answer: Gelatin is often made from pork or from animals not slaughtered Islamically, so many Muslims avoid it unless it is marked halal or is plant-based. Scholars differ on whether the manufacturing process changes gelatin into a completely new substance (called istihala, meaning full transformation). The Shafi'i school says pork gelatin stays forbidden, while some scholars from other schools and an AMJA scholar accept the transformation argument. A simple beginner approach is to choose halal-certified or plant-based products (agar, pectin) when you can, and not to panic over something you ate before you knew.
differences: The Shafi'i school does not accept that processing changes pork gelatin. The Hanafi and Maliki schools and one Hanbali view accept full transformation more broadly.

question: My family serves regular supermarket meat. Can I eat it?
answer: This is one of the biggest differences of opinion among Muslims in North America. Some scholars say the meat of Christians and Jews (People of the Book) is allowed under Quran 5:5. An AMJA scholar holds that you need not ask how it was slaughtered when you do not know, but that this does not apply when you know it was not properly slaughtered. Many other scholars and Canadian certifiers only accept zabiha (Islamically slaughtered) meat. You do not need to settle this debate at the dinner table. Many converts simply take the vegetarian dishes, fish or sides at family meals, or bring a halal dish to share, and ask their local imam which view to follow at home.
differences: Some scholars accept the meat of Christians and Jews under Quran 5:5. Many others accept only zabiha meat.

question: We share a kitchen and the family cooks pork. Are the dishes and pans okay for me?
answer: Yes, in general. A SeekersGuidance answer by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani explains that washing, even once, removes the impurity, whether by hand or in a dishwasher, with or without soap. Over-checking this is described as baseless misgivings (waswasa), which the religion discourages. If you can, keep one pan and a set of utensils of your own for cooking, which also avoids tension. The food itself is what matters: the cook being non-Muslim does not make permissible food forbidden.
differences: Details of purification differ by school. This answer follows the Hanafi school, and some schools are stricter about pork.

question: Can I ask my employer or school for time to pray?
answer: Yes. Human rights law in Canada protects religious practice at work and at school, and which law applies depends on who your employer is, not only on where you live. In Ontario, the Human Rights Code requires employers and schools to accommodate sincerely held religious practices unless it causes undue hardship, which is a high bar limited to cost, outside funding, and health and safety. You do not have to prove that prayer is 'mandatory' in Islam. Sincerity is the test. If you work for a federally regulated employer such as a bank, airline, Canada Post or a federal department, the Canadian Human Rights Act applies instead, and other provinces such as Alberta and British Columbia also protect religion at work. Quebec is different for some public-sector jobs: its laicity law bars people in the roles it lists from wearing religious symbols at work and limits prayer in places run by the public bodies it lists, so check the current law before you rely on this. Most prayers fit into a normal day because each one has a window, and a prayer break, including washing before prayer (wudu), usually takes about 10 to 15 minutes. Ask early, in writing if you can, and be specific: which prayers fall in your hours, how long each takes, what space you need, and whether you need time for Friday prayer. Offer options such as using part of a break or staying a little later. The Ontario Human Rights Commission says the person asking should explain their needs, answer reasonable questions and help find a solution. You can also share a guide written for managers, such as the one from the Muslim Federal Employees Network. This is general information, not legal advice.

question: What about Friday prayer and fasting in Ramadan at work?
answer: The Ontario Human Rights Commission gives examples of both. For Friday prayer, options include a longer lunch, staggered hours or making the time up. For Ramadan, it mentions schedule changes such as working through lunch to leave early for breaking the fast, without loss of pay. You can also ask for religious holidays like Eid off without being forced to use vacation days, for example by using lieu time or swapping shifts. Start with a friendly conversation and offer a solution; many managers are glad to help when they can see how the work still gets done.

question: I live in Quebec. Are the rules different?
answer: Partly. Quebec's Act respecting the laicity of the State (often called Bill 21) bans people in certain public-sector roles listed in the law from wearing religious symbols, such as a hijab, while working. The law was expanded in 2025 and 2026, including rules about prayer in school buildings during class hours, and the law now also covers subsidised daycare workers and limits religious practice in public institutions. A Supreme Court of Canada challenge was heard in 2026. Because this is changing fast, check the current law or a legal clinic before making a job decision.

question: My team socials are always at a bar. What do I do?
answer: You do not have to drink, and you can still be part of the team. Many scholars advise not sitting at a table where alcohol is being served, based on a hadith in Tirmidhi, and SeekersGuidance advises politely declining gatherings centred on alcohol and suggesting alternatives. At work, try offering a different plan (a lunch, a coffee, a board game night) or join for the first part of an event held somewhere other than a bar. If someone asks, a short answer works: 'I don't drink, but I'd love to come to the lunch.' Scholars differ on events where alcohol is present but not the focus, so ask your imam about your specific situation.
differences: Scholars differ on how strict to be about events where alcohol is present but is not the focus.

question: Do I have to stop shaking hands with people of the opposite sex?
answer: Scholars disagree on this, so nobody should shame you for either choice. Most scholars of the four schools say a man and a woman who are not close family should not shake hands, based on reports such as Aisha's statement in Sahih Muslim that the Prophet never touched a woman's hand when taking the pledge. Egypt's official fatwa body, Dar al-Ifta, says it is a disputed question and that a Muslim may follow the scholars who allow a handshake without desire, especially in non-Muslim countries to avoid embarrassing others. If you decide not to shake hands, an AMJA scholar advises explaining that you avoid it out of respect, not disdain, and if you get caught in a moment you could not avoid, you simply ask Allah's forgiveness. A friendly script: put your hand on your heart, smile, and say, 'I don't shake hands for religious reasons, but it's really nice to meet you.' Ask your local imam which view to follow, especially if your job makes this hard.
differences: Most scholars of the four schools say it is not permitted (the Hanafi and Hanbali schools allow it with elderly women). Some scholars are more lenient in unavoidable work situations. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta says a Muslim may follow the scholars who permit a handshake without desire.

question: I have tattoos from before Islam. Do I need to remove them?
answer: No, not if removal is costly or harmful. Scholars at AMJA explain that what you did before Islam is forgiven, and that the Prophet told a new Muslim, 'You became Muslim with all those good deeds' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1436). You do not have to cover them when you pray. You may cover them in the masjid if you like, but do not be hard on yourself, and uncovering them in hot weather is fine.

question: I already have a dog. Do I have to give it up?
answer: Scholars generally discourage keeping dogs as indoor pets, while allowing working dogs such as guard dogs, and some advise keeping a dog outside or rehoming it; this is where AMJA and a SeekersGuidance Hanafi answer both land. The Maliki school is known for a more lenient view on dogs. Please do not make a sudden decision that hurts your family or the animal. Talk to a scholar about your situation, especially if the dog belongs to other family members, is a service dog, or is part of a shared home.
differences: The Maliki school is known for a more lenient view on dogs.

question: Do I have to stop listening to music?
answer: Scholars have disagreed about music for centuries, and it is not something you need to settle in your first weeks. Most scholars of the four schools hold that musical instruments are not allowed, apart from the duff (a hand drum), which the Hanafi school and others allow. They cite a report in Sahih al-Bukhari (5590), whose chain scholars also discuss. Singing with good words is fine. Some scholars, such as Imam al-Ghazali, and today Egypt's Dar al-Ifta, allow music whose words and setting are clean, with no indecent lyrics, no alcohol and nothing that stirs up desire. Everyone agrees that lyrics promoting sin are a problem. An AMJA scholar adds that hearing music you did not choose, like in a store or on the news, is not held against you. Focus first on prayer and the basics, then learn the views with a teacher you trust.
differences: Most scholars of the four schools restrict musical instruments. Some scholars, including Egypt's Dar al-Ifta, permit clean music with conditions.

question: I have a mortgage, credit card or car loan with interest. What now?
answer: The Quran forbids interest (riba) and permits trade (2:275), and it tells believers to give up outstanding interest (2:278-279). Many new Muslims already have loans with interest, and you do not need to panic or break contracts overnight. Keep paying what you owe, pay credit cards in full each month so you do not pay interest, and avoid new interest-based debt where you can. For a home, many scholars, including SeekersGuidance teachers, say a conventional interest mortgage should be avoided and an Islamic home-financing option chosen, ideally one checked by a board of qualified scholars. Such products differ in the contract (ownership, risk and a fixed known price) even when the monthly cost looks similar. A few official bodies, such as Egypt's Dar al-Ifta, allow a bank home loan as a form of sale. Before you change an existing mortgage or sign anything new, ask a qualified scholar and a financial adviser.
differences: Many scholars say conventional interest mortgages are not permitted and advise a certified Islamic alternative. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta treats a bank home loan as a permitted sale (murabaha).

question: Are lottery tickets, sports betting or office pools okay?
answer: Gambling is forbidden in the Quran, which lists it with intoxicants as something to avoid (5:90). That includes lottery tickets, casino games, sports betting and paid office pools where everyone puts money in and one person wins. Free prize draws where you pay nothing are a separate question that scholars discuss. If a co-worker asks you to join a pool, a light answer works: 'I'll sit this one out, but good luck!'
differences: Scholars differ on free promotional draws where you pay nothing.

question: I smoke or vape. Do I have to quit right away?
answer: Many contemporary scholars consider smoking forbidden or strongly disliked because of its proven harm, while others call it disliked; SeekersGuidance summarises both views. Cannabis is treated like alcohol because it intoxicates. Quitting nicotine is hard, and Islam values steady progress. Health Canada and your doctor can help with quitting supports, and you can make it part of your new start without shame.
differences: Some scholars say smoking is forbidden (haram) and others say it is disliked (makruh).

question: Do I still have to respect my parents if they are not Muslim?
answer: Yes, very much. The Quran tells believers to honour their parents and, even if parents push them to worship other than Allah, not to obey in that but still to 'keep their company in this world courteously' (31:15). When Asma bint Abi Bakr asked the Prophet whether she should keep good relations with her non-Muslim mother, he said, 'Yes, keep good relation with her' (Sahih al-Bukhari 2620). The Quran also says Allah does not forbid kindness and fairness toward people who have not fought you (60:8). Being a kinder, more patient son or daughter is often the strongest thing a new Muslim can show their family.

question: I still live with my parents and they don't like my new practices. How do I handle it?
answer: Keep the non-negotiables small and firm, and be flexible about the rest. Shaykh Abdullah Anik Misra, a convert from Toronto, advises being firm about prayer and fasting, avoiding debates, helping around the house, going out with the family, and not listing every rule, only the major ones like not drinking or eating unlawful meat. He also suggests being vegetarian at home if needed, and dressing neatly so your family sees you are still you. Keep your room feeling like home rather than, in his words, a different country, and give your parents time. If home is not safe, your safety comes first; see our red flags and staying safe guide and the Government of Canada safety planning page.

question: Someone told me I should cut off my non-Muslim family. Is that true?
answer: No. Keeping family ties is required whatever your relatives' religion, as SeekersGuidance explains, and the early Muslims were themselves converts with non-Muslim families. The Prophet told Asma bint Abi Bakr to keep good relations with her non-Muslim mother. If a relative is harmful, you may reduce contact and keep up the relationship in other ways, such as calls, small gifts and making dua for them. If anyone in a community pressures you to cut off your family, that is a warning sign worth talking about with a trusted imam or counsellor.

question: I became Muslim but my husband or wife did not. What happens to my marriage?
answer: Please do not make a sudden decision, and nobody should pressure you to leave your home quickly. If you are a husband and your wife is Christian or Jewish, a 2019 Shafi'i answer from SeekersGuidance says your marriage stays valid, though its footnote adds a strict Shafi'i condition on who counts as Christian or Jewish. If you are a wife and your husband is not Muslim, AMJA's Family Code (article 42) says intimacy stops and the marriage is suspended during the waiting period (iddah): it continues if he becomes Muslim, and otherwise she may choose to end it. Your civil marriage is a legal marriage in Canada and ends only through a court. You are not alone: in a US survey of 618 converts (Yaqeen Institute, 2025), 29.6% of married men and 13% of married women had a spouse who was not Muslim.
differences: The schools differ on when the waiting period starts, when the marriage ends and what role a judge has. The European Council for Fatwa and Research allows a wife to stay if her husband does not obstruct her practice. If you are a husband and your wife follows another religion or none, the rules are different. If your spouse later becomes Muslim, ask a scholar whether a new nikah is needed.

question: Can I keep my non-Muslim friends?
answer: Yes. SeekersGuidance explains that befriending non-Muslims is neither forbidden nor disliked, and that the verses sometimes quoted against it (such as 5:51) are about alliances that harm the Muslim community, not everyday friendship. The Quran encourages kindness and fairness to people who have not fought you (60:8). Good friends who respect your changes are a blessing. It is also healthy to add a few Muslim friends over time; in one survey, most converts made friends at their local masjid.

question: People keep telling me I need to get married soon. Do I have to?
answer: No one has the right to rush you. Marriage is a big decision, and it is fine to take time to settle into your faith, learn, and get to know people properly first. If you feel pressured, say you are not ready, and talk to a qualified imam you trust about your own situation. If someone threatens you or tries to control who you see, that is not acceptable, and you can get help (in danger, call 9-1-1).

question: What do the words of the Shahada actually mean?
answer: The Shahada has two parts. 'Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah' means 'I bear witness that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah.' It says two things at once: you turn away from worshipping anything else, and you give your worship to Allah alone. 'Wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah' means 'and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.' He was a human being, not divine, and you accept him as the final messenger whose example shows you how to live and worship. You do not need to understand every detail on day one. Knowing this core meaning is enough to start.

question: I said the Shahada on my own, with nobody there. Am I really Muslim?
answer: Yes. Scholars explain that witnesses are not needed for your Shahada to be valid between you and Allah. If you believed it and said it sincerely, you are Muslim, even if you were alone. Witnesses and a certificate are about the community recognising you, for example for a marriage at a masjid or for Hajj later. If you would like that, you can say the Shahada again at a local masjid whenever you are ready. There is no rush.

question: Do I need a Shahada certificate?
answer: You do not need a certificate to be Muslim. Some people ask for one later because it can be needed for a marriage at a masjid, for Umrah or Hajj applications, or other paperwork. Some masjids issue a certificate signed by their imam on request. Ask your local masjid office whether they do this and what they need from you.

question: What are the five pillars of Islam?
answer: The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said that Islam is built on five things. They are: the Shahada (declaring your faith), Salah (the five daily prayers), Zakat (a yearly charity paid by those with enough savings), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), and Hajj (the pilgrimage to Makkah once in a lifetime, for those who are able). Think of them as the pillars that hold up a building. You have already stood up the first one by saying the Shahada. Prayer is the next one to work on. Zakat and Hajj only apply when your circumstances require them.
differences: How zakat is calculated differs between the schools. Our zakat guide covers the details.

question: I have said the Shahada. What comes next?
answer: The step after the Shahada is prayer. When the Prophet (peace be upon him) sent a companion to teach people, he told him to teach the Shahada first, and once they accepted it, to teach the five daily prayers. Prayer needs a simple wash first (wudu), and many scholars also advise a full-body wash (ghusl) after becoming Muslim. So a gentle order is: understand your Shahada, learn wudu, then learn one short prayer and build from there. You do not need to learn everything this week.
differences: The schools differ on whether ghusl after becoming Muslim is required or recommended.

question: Do I have to do all five pillars straight away?
answer: No. The Shahada is done. Prayer is the pillar to start learning now, one step at a time. Fasting comes when Ramadan arrives. Zakat only applies once your savings are above a set minimum, and our zakat guide explains how that works. Hajj is only required once in a lifetime, and only if you are physically and financially able. So for most new Muslims, the real focus in the first weeks is faith and prayer.
differences: The way the zakat minimum (nisab) is worked out differs. Our zakat guide covers the details.

question: What do Muslims believe? What are the six articles of faith?
answer: When the angel Jibril (Gabriel) asked the Prophet (peace be upon him) what faith is, he answered with six things: belief in Allah, His angels, His revealed books, His messengers, the Last Day, and Allah's decree of good and bad. Many of these will already feel familiar if you grew up Christian or Jewish, such as angels, prophets and a day of judgement. You can learn each one slowly. Our Core beliefs page walks through them.

question: What is shirk, and why do Muslims take it so seriously?
answer: Shirk means giving any part of worship, or any quality that belongs only to God, to someone or something else. Worship includes prayer, calling on someone for help beyond human ability, and devotion. Islam's central message, and the message of all the prophets, is that worship belongs to Allah alone. The Quran calls shirk the gravest wrong. It also makes clear that Allah forgives anyone who turns away from it, so this is about where you are heading, not about punishing yourself over the past.
differences: Scholars agree on the core meaning. They describe the lesser forms in different ways.

question: I used to pray to Jesus. Was that wrong, and will I be punished for it?
answer: Many people who come to Islam from Christianity ask this. Muslims love and honour Jesus (peace be upon him) as one of the greatest prophets, and the Quran describes him saying, 'I am the servant of Allah.' From now on, Muslims direct prayer to Allah alone, not to Jesus, Mary or the saints, and not 'in Jesus's name.' What you did before Islam is forgiven: the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said that Islam wipes out what came before it, and the Quran says past wrongs are forgiven for those who stop. You do not need to carry guilt about the past. Just turn to Allah directly now.

question: What happens to the sins I committed before I became Muslim?
answer: They are wiped away. When the companion Amr ibn al-As hesitated to accept Islam because of his past, the Prophet (peace be upon him) asked him, 'Are you not aware that Islam wipes out all the previous misdeeds?' The Quran also says that for those who repent, believe and do good, Allah replaces their bad deeds with good ones. You are starting with a clean page. If someone you wronged is still owed something, such as money, it is good to make that right when you can.
differences: Scholars discuss whether rights owed to other people, such as debts, are cancelled. The last sentence follows the cautious view.

question: Will the good things I did before Islam count for anything?
answer: Yes. A companion named Hakim ibn Hizam asked the Prophet (peace be upon him) about the charity and kindness to family he had done before becoming Muslim. The Prophet told him, 'You became Muslim with all those good deeds.' So your past kindness is not lost.

readMore.label: Your first day as a Muslim

question: I have made mistakes since becoming Muslim. How do I repent?
answer: Tawbah (repentance) means turning back to Allah. It has three simple parts: feel sorry for what you did, stop doing it, and sincerely intend not to return to it. If you wronged a person, try to put it right with them. You can repent at any time, in your own words and in any language. The Prophet (peace be upon him) told us Allah is more pleased with a servant's repentance than a traveller who finds his lost camel in the desert. Slipping again does not close the door; keep coming back.

question: I believe, but I am not praying five times a day yet. Am I still a Muslim?
answer: Yes. You became Muslim through your belief and your Shahada. Islam then asks you to put that belief into practice, and prayer is the most important practice, so it is worth working towards steadily. Scholars who guide converts advise doing what you can now, without deliberately neglecting prayer, and adding more as you learn. Pray the prayers you can, learn the rest step by step, and ask for help when you need it. Growth is expected, not instant perfection.
differences: Scholars differ on the legal status of someone who stops praying altogether. This answer is about a learner who is working towards prayer, and gives no ruling on that question.

question: Do I have to change my name?
answer: No. Most companions of the Prophet (peace be upon him) kept their names. You only need to change a name if its meaning goes against Islam, for example a name meaning 'servant of the Messiah' or a name that belongs only to God, or if it has a bad meaning. You should keep your family name, as Islam values staying connected to your father's lineage. Some people like to take an Arabic name as a nickname or a legal change, and that is fine too, but it is your choice.

question: Do I have to be circumcised? (for men)
answer: You do not need to be circumcised to become Muslim, and your Shahada is valid either way. After that, schools of Islamic law differ: some consider male circumcision strongly recommended, others consider it required. For an adult, health matters too, so talk to a doctor as well as a qualified scholar before deciding anything. Please do not let this worry stop you from praying or coming to the masjid.
differences: The Maliki school treats it as a sunnah, and other sources treat it as required.

question: Do I have to tell people that I am Muslim?
answer: No. Announcing your conversion is not a condition of being Muslim. You can take your time and decide who to tell, when, and how. Many converts start with one person they trust. If you think telling someone could put you at risk, your safety comes first; our family guide has safety resources.

question: Do I have to know Arabic to be Muslim?
answer: No. Not knowing Arabic does not make you any less Muslim, and most Muslims in the world are not Arabic speakers. Your dua (personal prayers) can be in English or any language. The five daily prayers include a few short Arabic passages, mainly Surah al-Fatiha, and you can learn these a little at a time. Until you know them, scholars describe ways to pray while you learn; see the next question.

question: Is saying the Shahada enough, or do I need to do something else to become Muslim?
answer: Sincerely believing and saying the Shahada is what makes you Muslim. There is no baptism-like ceremony, no fee, and no requirement to have a certificate, change your name, or learn Arabic first. Everything else, like prayer and learning the Quran, is part of living as a Muslim and comes step by step after that.

question: There is so much to learn. Where do I even start?
answer: You do not have to learn everything at once. In your first days, the basics are your belief in one God, the Shahada, and learning to pray. After that, add one thing at a time: Al-Fatihah and a few short chapters, then the meaning of what you recite, then fasting and daily life. The Prophet said the most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant, even if it is small. Five focused minutes a day is a real start. Self-paced courses such as New Muslim Academy let you start when you are ready and go at your own speed, and they have forums where you can ask questions. If someone hands you a long list of rules on your first day, it is fine to say you are taking it step by step. You have a lifetime to keep learning.

question: How can I tell if an online source about Islam is reliable?
answer: Ask three questions. Who wrote it, and are they a named scholar or an established organisation? Does it give its evidence, such as a Quran verse with chapter and verse, or a hadith with its collection and number? And does it say how strong that hadith is? Scholars sort hadith by their chain of narrators into grades such as sahih (authentic) and da'if (weak). Be careful with quote images, anonymous posts, videos that tell you to reject all teachers except one, and anything that makes you feel afraid or rushed. When in doubt, take the question to a qualified local imam.

question: Should I sign up for a course? Which one?
answer: You do not need a course in your first week. Once you are praying and feel a little settled, a free structured course can give you a clear order to follow. New Muslim Academy is free and made for people who have just become Muslim, starting with wudu and prayer. You need a free account to use it. SeekersGuidance runs free Level One live classes. Pick one course at a time and finish it before starting another. If a course asks for money up front, pushes you to cut off other teachers, or wants personal details that seem unnecessary, pause and ask someone you trust.

question: Do I have to go on Hajj right away?
answer: No. Hajj is required once in a lifetime for those who are able, physically and financially, and the Quran ties it to ability. For a new Muslim, it is something to learn about and look forward to, not a pressure. Umrah, the smaller pilgrimage, is a separate act from Hajj.
differences: The schools differ on whether Hajj must be done as soon as you are able or may be delayed.

question: How do I book Hajj or Umrah safely from Canada?
answer: Start with the official sources. Read the Government of Canada travel advice for Saudi Arabia, which currently advises against non-essential travel, and check it again close to your trip. Hajj needs a Hajj visa and is arranged through the Saudi Ministry's official Nusuk platform or its authorized providers. Umrah can be done on other visa types. Be careful with anyone offering cheap or guaranteed Hajj places, asking for cash deposits, or pressuring you to decide fast, and report suspected fraud to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

question: As a woman, can I go on Umrah alone, and what if my period starts?
answer: Saudi rules now let women of any age travel for Hajj or Umrah without a male guardian (mahram), according to the Government of Canada. Whether a woman should travel for pilgrimage without a mahram is a separate religious question on which scholars differ, so ask a scholar you trust. If your period starts, you can do everything except the tawaf around the Kaaba, which you do once you are clean, as the Prophet told Aisha.
differences: The schools differ on whether a woman needs a mahram for pilgrimage. What to do if you must leave before becoming clean for tawaf is a detailed question for a scholar.

question: Can I still spend Christmas with my family?
answer: Many scholars say yes, as long as you are there for your family and not taking part in religious rituals. Staying close to your family is part of Islam, and a SeekersGuidance answer says attending is part of keeping family ties, while quietly not joining religious activities such as prayers or a church service. Other scholars are stricter and advise visiting family at another time instead of joining the festivity itself. Some converts choose a middle path: come for the meal and the company, eat what is halal for you, skip the religious parts politely, and make the visit about your family. You can say, 'I'm so glad to be here with you all. I'll sit out the prayer, but I wouldn't miss dinner.' Where alcohol is served, views differ, and the stricter view says not to attend. Talk to a local imam if you are unsure.
differences: Views range from attending the family meal while avoiding the rites (SeekersGuidance), to declining the festivity itself (AMJA 77225, about a friend's invitation), to visiting family at other times but not joining the festivities (Islamweb). IslamQA also takes a stricter view.

question: Can I give or accept Christmas presents?
answer: Accepting gifts from family, neighbours and co-workers is widely considered fine because gift-giving is a social custom, and accepting gifts is a Sunnah practice. SeekersGuidance also allows giving presents to family in December to strengthen ties, in your own dignified way. An AMJA scholar adds that you may decline a gift tied directly to religious ritual, and suggests celebrating other occasions with family, such as birthdays and graduations, so they feel your love. Some scholars advise not having a Christmas tree in a Muslim's own home.
differences: Some scholars discourage timing gifts to the holiday.

question: Someone says 'Merry Christmas' to me. What should I say back?
answer: Scholars differ here. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta says congratulating non-Muslims on their occasions is allowed, especially with family and colleagues, as long as it does not mean agreeing with their beliefs. Other scholars, such as Shaykh Jamaal Zarabozo for AMJA, advise not saying 'Merry Christmas' and instead replying warmly in another way, like 'So how have you been?' or 'I hope to see you again soon.' Either way, a warm, kind reply matters more than the exact words. Ask your local imam which view to follow.
differences: Some scholars allow the greeting and others advise a different warm reply.

question: Is Thanksgiving okay?
answer: Some scholars, including teachers at SeekersGuidance, see Canadian Thanksgiving as a national and family occasion rather than a religious one. SeekersGuidance says attending a Thanksgiving dinner with family is permitted, especially when there is benefit in going and harm in staying away, and that national holidays are fine if you do not treat them as religiously sacred. Some AMJA scholars disagree and say Muslims should not celebrate it. If you go, the usual guidance applies: eat what is halal for you, and politely skip any alcohol.
differences: SeekersGuidance teachers permit it. Some AMJA scholars say Muslims should not celebrate it.

question: What about Halloween, especially for my kids?
answer: Most scholars whose answers we checked advise not joining Halloween because of its origins. Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, answering a parent in Canada, suggests giving your children treats or taking them somewhere special instead, and checking with local scholars. An AMJA scholar, answering a convert mother who wanted to share her own childhood fun, suggests putting that energy into the two Eids with sweets, gifts and dressing up. It is okay to feel a little sad about letting go of a tradition you loved; building new family traditions around the Eids helps.
differences: Some scholars treat handing out candy at the door as a separate question.

question: Can I celebrate birthdays?
answer: Scholars differ. Some, including an AMJA scholar, say birthdays are generally treated as social occasions and are not explicitly forbidden, so an occasional celebration, especially for children, is no harm. Others say to avoid birthday parties as an imitation of other traditions: one AMJA scholar says they are not permissible, and a SeekersGuidance teacher leans that way. If your family throws you a party, you do not need to cause a scene; you can enjoy the time with them and ask your imam about your own practice going forward.
differences: This is a clear, documented difference between scholars.

question: Can I go to church with my family for a wedding, a funeral, Easter or Christmas?
answer: This is one of the most common questions from new Muslims. Joining in the worship of another religion is where scholars draw a clear line. SeekersGuidance says a Muslim should not actively celebrate another religion's religious festival, and that at family gatherings one should quietly not take part in religious activities. That is different from spending time with your family, eating with them, or learning about their traditions. Scholars answer differently about being present in a church. Some official fatwa bodies say you may attend a relative's funeral, even in a church, as part of keeping family ties. Some scholars allow the family gathering but advise against attending the church service itself, and others take a stricter view. All of these answers fit the Quran's call to keep treating your family with kindness. A kind way to say it: 'I love you and I'll be there for lunch. I won't join the service, because I pray differently now.' Because your situation matters, ask a local imam or scholar you trust before the event.
differences: Views range widely. Some bodies, such as Egypt's Dar al-Ifta and an AMJA scholar, allow attending a funeral. SeekersGuidance Hanafi answers allow the family gathering but not the church service without strong need. IslamQA takes a strict view. The one wedding-specific source found (IslamQA) is strict.

question: There will be alcohol at the family party. Should I still go?
answer: Scholars generally advise against sitting where alcohol is being served, and SeekersGuidance says a gathering built around alcohol is not a place for a believer. They also stress staying kind and connected: offer to take the family out for a meal, visit before the party, or host something yourself. If you do go to a family event where some people drink, many converts sit with the non-drinkers, bring their own drinks, and leave before things get rowdy; ask your imam how this applies to your situation.
differences: Scholars differ on how strictly to apply this to family events where alcohol is present but not central.

question: Do I have to do qurbani for Eid al-Adha?
answer: Qurbani (also called udhiyah) is sacrificing an animal after the Eid al-Adha prayer, and the meat is shared, including with people in need. The Hanafi school says it is required for those above the zakat threshold. Most other scholars say it is strongly recommended. Canadian charities such as Islamic Relief Canada arrange it for donors. The Quran reminds us that it is our devotion, not the meat or blood, that reaches Allah.
differences: The Hanafi school says qurbani is required for those above the zakat minimum, and most other scholars say it is strongly recommended. Not cutting hair and nails beforehand is recommended or required depending on the school.

question: Do I pray during my period, and do I have to make those prayers up later?
answer: No. During your period (called hayd in Arabic), or bleeding after childbirth, you do not perform the five daily prayers, and you do not make them up afterwards. This is a mercy, not a punishment. The wives of the Prophet said they were never told to make up prayers missed during their periods. Once the bleeding ends and you have done the full-body wash (ghusl), you start praying again from the next prayer. If a prayer time had already started before your bleeding began, or your period ends before a prayer time is over, scholars say you may owe that prayer. Ask a knowledgeable woman teacher or imam how your school handles this, or if you are unsure whether your period has ended.
differences: Scholars agree on the basic rule. The schools differ on which prayers are owed when bleeding starts or stops partway through a prayer time, on the shortest and longest period lengths, and on irregular bleeding.

question: If my period comes during Ramadan, do I still fast? Do I owe those days?
answer: You do not fast while you are on your period, and a fast you started becomes void if your period begins before sunset. You make up those days later, one day for each day missed, ideally before the next Ramadan. You can still enjoy Ramadan in other ways: dua, dhikr, charity, helping prepare iftar, and attending gatherings.
differences: Scholars differ on what happens if the make-up is delayed past the next Ramadan without a reason. Some add fidyah, and the Hanafi school does not.

question: Can I read or recite the Quran during my period?
answer: Scholars genuinely differ here, so you will hear different answers. The Hanafi and Shafi'i schools say a woman on her period should not recite the Quran aloud, though she may listen to it, look at it and think about its meaning, and say Quranic phrases as dua or dhikr. The Maliki school allows recitation, and some later scholars allow recitation from memory as long as you do not touch a printed Quran. Ask the imam or teacher you learn with which view to follow, and do not feel guilty for following a recognised scholarly view.
differences: The Hanafi and Shafi'i schools say no recitation. The Maliki school allows recitation. Some contemporary scholars allow recitation from memory. The narration often quoted for the ban (Tirmidhi 131) is graded weak.

question: Can I touch the Quran, or use a Quran app on my phone, during my period?
answer: Most scholars say you should not touch a printed Arabic Quran (called a mushaf) while on your period. Many allow holding it with a separate cloth or cover, though schools differ on the details. Several scholars say a phone or tablet app is not a mushaf, so touching the screen is different, and AMJA gave this view for devices and tafsir books. The Hanafi school is stricter about touching printed translations and tafsir. If you are unsure, use an app or listen to recitation, and ask your teacher.
differences: Scholars differ on touching printed translations and tafsir, on using a covering, and on treating devices as different from a mushaf. Some scholars (AMJA 86681) permit touching the mushaf when there is a need, and NewMuslims.com allows touching translations.

question: Can I still make dua and dhikr while I am on my period?
answer: Yes. Dua (asking Allah in your own words, in any language) and dhikr (remembering Allah with phrases like SubhanAllah, Alhamdulillah, Allahu Akbar) are open to you at any time. You can also send blessings on the Prophet, listen to the Quran, give charity, and help others. Your connection with Allah does not pause during your period.
differences: Scholars agree on dua and dhikr in general. The schools checked allow Quranic verses said with the intention of dua.

question: Can I go to the masjid, a class, or Eid while on my period?
answer: You are welcome at Eid and community gatherings. The Prophet told women on their periods to come out for Eid and join the gathering, while staying away from the prayer rows themselves. Staying inside the main prayer hall of a masjid is where scholars differ: most schools say not to stay in it during your period, while some scholars allow it. Many Canadian centres have classrooms, halls and offices that are not part of the prayer hall, so ask the imam or office which rooms count as the masjid.
differences: Most schools say not to stay in the masjid prayer area, with different details on passing through. The narration 'I do not make the mosque lawful for a menstruating woman' (Abu Dawud 232) is graded weak by al-Albani.

question: How do I know my period has ended, and what do I do then?
answer: Your period has ended when the bleeding stops. Many women check with a white cloth or pad for either a clear or white discharge or complete dryness. Then you do the full-body wash (ghusl): make the intention, wash, and make sure water reaches your whole body and hair roots. After that you pray and, in Ramadan, fast as normal. The steps are the same as the ghusl on the Wudu and ghusl tool.
differences: The signs of purity, and how to treat brown or yellow discharge, differ between the schools.

question: I keep bleeding outside my normal period. Do I still pray?
answer: Not all bleeding counts as a period. Bleeding outside your usual period, or bleeding that goes past the longest period length, is called istihadah (irregular bleeding), and it does not stop you from praying. The Prophet told a woman with ongoing bleeding to stop praying only during her actual period, then wash and pray. In the Hanafi school, if bleeding runs past ten days, the days beyond your usual period length count as istihadah, so you keep praying and fasting as normal, and you can read the Quran and go to the masjid. If the bleeding is so constant that you cannot make wudu and pray a short obligatory prayer before it returns, you count as 'excused'. You then make one wudu when each prayer time begins, and that wudu lasts until the time ends, even if bleeding continues. Other schools set the details differently. Keep a simple record of when bleeding starts and stops, see a doctor about the cause, and ask a knowledgeable woman teacher or local scholar about your own pattern. You can ask for a female teacher if you prefer.
differences: The shortest and longest lengths of a period, and how to sort irregular bleeding, differ between the schools. The Shafi'i and other schools also differ from the Hanafi school on whether wudu is made for each prayer or for each prayer time.

question: What about bleeding after giving birth?
answer: Bleeding after childbirth is called nifas. The rules are the same as for a period: you do not pray or fast while it continues, you make up missed Ramadan fasts later, and you do not make up the prayers. Many scholars give forty days as the usual maximum, but if the bleeding stops earlier, you take ghusl and start praying again. New mothers should also follow their doctor's or midwife's advice about their health.
differences: The longest length of bleeding after birth differs between the schools.

question: Is my period a sign that I am spiritually impure or less of a Muslim?
answer: No. The Prophet told his wife Aisha, who was upset when her period came during Hajj, that it is something Allah has written for all the daughters of Adam. He would rest his head in her lap and recite the Quran while she was on her period. The break from prayer and fasting is a rule for a set time, not a judgement on you. You remain a full member of the community.

question: A mentor or teacher is making me uncomfortable. What can I do?
answer: Trust that feeling. A mentor should never ask for money, ask to meet alone in private places, pressure you about marriage, ask for photos, or tell you to keep things secret. You can stop meeting them at any time. Tell the program coordinator or another trusted person at the organisation, and if you are in danger or there has been a crime, call 9-1-1 or the police. If the person is connected to Revert Guide, you can report them to us through our get help page.

question: What are the five daily prayers called, and when do I pray them?
answer: The five daily prayers are Fajr (dawn), Dhuhr (just after midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (just after sunset) and Isha (night). Each one has a window: Fajr runs from dawn until sunrise, Dhuhr until Asr starts, Asr until sunset, Maghrib until Isha starts, and Isha until the middle of the night for most purposes. You can pray any time inside the window, so you do not need to be exact to the minute. The times move every day with the sun, so use a timetable from your local masjid or the prayer times page on this site.
differences: The schools differ on when Asr begins (the Hanafi start is later) and on the latest time for Isha.

question: How many units (rak'ahs) does each prayer have?
answer: A rak'ah is one cycle of standing, bowing and two prostrations. Fajr has 2, Dhuhr has 4, Asr has 4, Maghrib has 3 and Isha has 4. That makes 17 obligatory units a day. Many Muslims also pray extra voluntary units around these, but those can wait while you learn.
differences: Scholars agree on the obligatory counts. Shortening prayers while travelling is a separate topic.

question: Why do different apps and masjids show different prayer times?
answer: Fajr and Isha depend on how dark the sky is, and scholars and astronomers measure that in different ways. Apps use different settings, called calculation methods, such as ISNA (15 degrees) or Muslim World League (18 degrees for Fajr). The Fiqh Council of North America says no single method is exact for every place, and suggests that people who can observe dawn and dusk may add a few minutes of caution, as a recommendation, not a requirement. Differences between methods can be large, sometimes more than an hour in summer in Canada, and they are not a sign that you prayed wrongly. If you pray with a local masjid, following its timetable keeps things simple.
differences: 13, 15 and 18 degree settings and seasonal methods are all in use.

question: Which prayer time method should I use in Canada?
answer: The Fiqh Council of North America published a recommendation of 13 degrees for Fajr and Isha in Canada, while its newer article describes 15 degrees as a good middle approximation. Some communities use the Moonsighting Committee method, which changes with the season. The simplest choice is to follow the timetable of the masjid you attend.
differences: Methods differ, and the two Fiqh Council of North America articles do not agree on Canada.

question: I live far north and in summer Isha is very late and Fajr is very early. What do I do?
answer: Above roughly 48.5 degrees of latitude (for the 18 degree setting), the summer sky may never get dark enough for the usual Fajr and Isha settings. Calculation methods handle this in different ways, for example by using seasonal estimates or a portion of the night. Ask your local masjid which timetable it follows. This is a question to take to your local imam, and it is a known situation, not a mistake on your part.
differences: Several methods exist for high latitudes.

question: I can't read or recite Arabic yet. Can I still pray?
answer: Yes. Many people start praying before they can read a single Arabic letter, and scholars describe ways to pray while you learn. One widely taught option is to say simple Arabic phrases of remembrance in place of the recitation you have not memorised yet, such as SubhanAllah (Glory be to Allah), Alhamdulillah (Praise be to Allah), La ilaha illallah (There is no god but Allah) and Allahu Akbar (Allah is greater). A hadith reports the Prophet teaching these words to a man who said he could not memorise any Quran, and SeekersGuidance says this approach is valid in the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools. Meanwhile, learn the opening chapter (Al-Fatiha) a line at a time by listening and repeating. All four schools recite it in Arabic in prayer, though they differ on its exact legal status. Allah does not ask a soul for more than it can bear (Quran 2:286). Ask a local imam which option to follow.
differences: The Hanafi school also accepts reciting the meaning in your own language for someone who cannot yet recite Arabic. The Shafi'i school uses Arabic remembrance phrases instead and, failing that, standing silently. The Maliki and Hanbali schools hold that recitation in another language is not valid.

question: Can I say my prayer in English?
answer: The schools of law answer this differently. In the Hanafi school, someone who cannot yet recite Arabic, such as a new Muslim, may recite a translation of Quran verses. The Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali schools do not accept recitation in another language. A SeekersGuidance answer calls short Arabic phrases of remembrance, like SubhanAllah, the more cautious option because it is valid in both the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools. Whatever you do for now, keep learning the Arabic of Al-Fatiha gradually.
differences: The schools answer this differently, as described above.

question: Can I read the words from a card or my phone while I pray?
answer: You can practise with a printed card before and after prayer. Reading from a book or screen during the prayer itself is a point of difference: the Hanafi school counts holding a Quran and reading from it in prayer as strongly disliked, while some beginner courses suggest reading from paper for a short time while memorising. A safe middle path is to memorise the short phrases first and use a card only outside prayer. Ask your local imam what your school allows.
differences: The Hanafi school dislikes reading from a mushaf in prayer. The Shafi'i school allows a learner to read al-Fatiha from a mushaf in prayer.

question: What is the simplest prayer I can start with this week?
answer: Start with the shape. Stand facing the qibla and say Allahu Akbar. Say what you know (a short phrase of remembrance if you do not know Al-Fatiha yet), bow, stand up, prostrate twice with a short sitting in between. That is one rak'ah. When the Prophet taught a man who prayed badly, he told him to recite what he knew of the Quran and to be calm and settled in each position. Calm and settled matters more than speed.
differences: What to say while you learn depends on the view in the question about praying before you know any Arabic.

question: How do I build up from one rak'ah to the full five prayers?
answer: Go in small steps. Pray all five daily prayers in the simple form while you learn. The steps below are about what you say and add, not which prayers you pray. First learn the positions and the phrases said in each. Then pray Fajr, which is two rak'ahs, with the phrases you know. Next add the sitting and the tashahhud after the second rak'ah, then learn how a three-unit prayer (Maghrib) and a four-unit prayer (Dhuhr, Asr, Isha) continue after that sitting. Replace the phrases of remembrance with Al-Fatiha and a short surah as you memorise them. Each step is a real prayer, not a rehearsal.

question: What do I say in each position of the prayer?
answer: Opening: Allahu Akbar (Allah is greater). Standing: Al-Fatiha, then a short surah. Bowing (ruku): Subhana Rabbiyal Azim (Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great). Rising: Sami Allahu liman hamidah (Allah hears whoever praises Him), then Rabbana wa lakal hamd (Our Lord, to You is praise). Prostration (sujud): Subhana Rabbiyal A'la (Glory be to my Lord, the Most High). Sitting between prostrations: Rabbighfir li (My Lord, forgive me). Final sitting: the tashahhud, then blessings on the Prophet, then As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah to the right and left.
differences: Wording varies slightly between narrations and schools, for example in the tashahhud. Several authentic wordings exist, so follow your teacher.

question: Do I have to make up the prayers from before I became Muslim?
answer: No. Prayers from before you became Muslim are not owed. Some scholars, for example in the Hanafi school, say a convert who had no idea yet that prayer was an obligation is not held to make up that time. Once you know, the aim is to start praying, even in a simple form, rather than waiting until you feel ready.
differences: Scholars agree that prayers from before Islam are not owed. The point about not yet knowing prayer was an obligation is a Hanafi position, and schools may differ.

question: I missed a prayer. What should I do now?
answer: Pray it as soon as you remember, then carry on with your day. The Prophet said that whoever forgets a prayer should pray it when they remember it. If you have missed many prayers since becoming Muslim, a teacher can help you set a small, steady make-up plan. Missing prayers is a reason to return, not a reason to give up.
differences: The schools differ on deliberately missed prayers and on praying sunnah prayers while making up.
